title: PEDOT:PSS-Coated Magnetoelastic Sensors for Highly Sensitive Wireless Humidity Sensing
authors: Wenderson R. F. Silva, Robson C. O. Guedes, Gilberto Rodrigues-Junior, Eduarda P. M. Campos, Angelo Malachias, Joaquim B. S. Mendes
abstract: Magnetoelastic (ME) resonators provide an attractive platform for passive and wireless sensing, particularly for monitoring relative humidity (RH) in sealed or hard-to-access environments. In this work, we introduce ME humidity sensors functionalized with poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) sulfonate (PEDOT), marking the first application of this conductive polymer in ME-based humidity sensing. PEDOT films were deposited onto Metglas resonators via a simple drop-casting process, producing uniform and mechanically stable coatings. Comprehensive structural and morphological characterization by SEM, EDX, Raman spectroscopy, AFM/KPFM, and XRD confirmed the structural integrity of the polymer and revealed humidity-induced swelling of the PSS-rich domains, accompanied by enhanced polymer-chain mobility and an increase in the lamellar spacing from 23.5 Å to 24.2 Å at 95% RH. These structural changes directly affected the dynamic response of the resonators, leading to a systematic resonance-frequency downshift driven by the combined effects of water adsorption, mass loading, and viscoelastic damping. The optimized device achieved a sensitivity of 155 Hz/% RH in the 20 - 70% RH range, outperforming previously reported ME humidity sensors, while exhibiting a resolution better than 0.1% RH together with excellent response and recovery times. These results establish PEDOT as a highly effective functional coating for magnetoelastic humidity sensors and demonstrate a simple, low-cost, wireless sensing platform with high sensitivity and strong potential for practical environmental and industrial monitoring applications.
summary: This work develops a novel, highly sensitive wireless humidity sensor by coating magnetoelastic resonators with PEDOT:PSS. The sensing mechanism exploits the dual effect of water adsorption causing both mass loading and viscoelastic damping within the polymer film. Characterization confirms that structural changes in the polymer directly translate into measurable resonance frequency shifts, achieving state-of-the-art sensitivity.
main_problem: Developing highly sensitive, wireless sensors for monitoring relative humidity (RH) in challenging environments.
main_result: The optimized PEDOT:PSS coated magnetoelastic sensor achieved a high sensitivity of 155 Hz/% RH in the 20-70% RH range, demonstrating a low-cost platform for environmental monitoring.
method: The study involved fabricating sensors by depositing PEDOT:PSS films onto Metglas resonators and measuring their resonance frequency shift while controlling ambient relative humidity.
model_or_system: The physical system is a magnetoelastic (ME) resonator functionalized with a conductive polymer coating (PEDOT:PSS). The sensing mechanism relies on the combined effects of mass loading (Sauerbrey effect) and viscoelastic damping caused by water adsorption into the polymer matrix.
key_observables: Resonance frequency shift ($\Delta f$), sensitivity ($155 	ext{ Hz/\%\ RH}$), resolution ($<0.1\% 	ext{RH}$), surface potential (KPFM), and XRD lamellar spacing change (23.5 Å to 24.2 Å).
important_parameters: Relative Humidity (RH) range (20-70% RH optimal), coating thickness ($0.5 \mu	ext{L}/	ext{mm}^2$), and temperature/annealing conditions.
main_assumptions: The resonance shift is modeled by combining the Sauerbrey equation for mass loading with viscoelastic damping effects, though the latter requires complex shear modulus considerations beyond simple approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the drop-casting process (Fig. 1), the measurement setup using a VNA in a controlled chamber (Fig. 2), and comparative data showing surface morphology (AFM/KPFM) and structural changes (XRD) across varying RH levels.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem definition $ightarrow$ material functionalization (PEDOT:PSS deposition) $ightarrow$ comprehensive characterization (structural, morphological, electronic) $ightarrow$ measurement of the frequency response to controlled humidity cycles $ightarrow$ quantitative analysis of sensitivity and performance metrics.
why_interesting: While not directly related to fundamental quantum dynamics, the study involves characterizing material changes (swelling, polymer mobility) at interfaces under environmental stimuli, which touches upon concepts relevant to open quantum systems or complex condensed matter interactions.
